THE PEOPLE &ND THE PARRS.

WHAT is the reason that Mr. GLADSTONE
and his Government will insist on embracing
every available opportunity to make them-
selves• unpopular? Most people thought that
they came to the work of the present session
with much more public distrust than there
Was any necessity for, simply because in the
past they had been meddling and muddling in
a. needlessly vexatious way with a number of
questions which, to satisfy the public, required
to be handled with an •extra wise carefulness.
One Member of the GoVernmenehad no sooner
dragged himself out of an unpleasant scrape,
than another had plunged into one, as if solely
for the purpose of keeping up public excite-
ment, and provoking public disapproval.
Mr. AYRTON'S is the most recent of these.
His Bill for the regulation of our Parks may
in some of its parts be wholesome and ne-
oessary, but it is impossible to read the whole
of its provisions without suspecting covert
intention inimical to public right.
The fight in Parliament when Mr. HARDY
fell foul of Mr. GLADSTONE, and Mr. GLAD-
S roNE returned that gentleman's rough-handed
cuffs with interest, to be attacked in turn by
Mr. DISRAELT, pointed with great clearness to
that,part of the measure in which our Minis-
ters, actual and possible; feel the strongest in-
terest. Of course most of the men on both
aides of the House would prefer that cabs were
nor permitted to penetrate within' the hal-
lowed precincts of the "drive" The fellow
With powdered poll and plush breeches is not a
oinfartithle or friendly neighbour to his poor
brother of the whip, whose only ornament is
his pendant badge. Nor would the poor in-
valid, trying to catch:a:mouthful of refreshing
air through the window of a
_hired 'cab, be a
desirable companion in idleness to the happy
occupant of the private barouche.
Ed though much might be said on this part
of the question, it is evident from what has
been uttered in the Rouse that the real desire
Is to put down the right of publio meet-
ing in the Parks, so that for the future
thn‘s who insist on airing their patriotism
there may be summorily 'dealt with by the
?ark authorities. Mr. HARDY WAS clearly
in a 'violent rage with Mr. GLADSTONE because
he did not ',heartily support the Conservative
Government in putting down the Hyde Park
.xacetings in 1867. Whilst Mr. GLADSTONE,
In his passionate reply, taunted the Govern-
Ecent of that day for having " plaoed the public
authority cif the Crown and the legislature at
tho feet of the populace of London." And
DISRA.ELT, following up with his usual
dexterity of flourish and thrust—though in this
instanee the aim was badly taken—showed
that popular meetings in Hyde Park were the
Offen,cos which he particularly:desired to see
DYeVented. No doubt cull of these gentlemen,

and Mr. ARYTON also, possess strong opinions
in favour of order and decorum in the parks.
Artistic taste and the refinements of culture
operate powerfully on them in prompting the
action upon which they have entered, in a
spirit not very friendly to each other. But
outside of all influences of this kind, there can
be no doubt that to drive discontented and un-
washed politicians out of the parks is their
main desire; and, however difficult united
action may be on other questions, on this they
will shake hands and co-operate. The bluster
of Mr. HARDY indicates this. Though he
dislikes Mr. GLAMTONE, and probably despises
Mr. AYRTON, he will help them to do what
they can for effecting this purpose. And Mr.
GLA.DSTONE, too, saw in the legal attitude of
the people, in reference to their right of meet-
ing in the parks, only the dominanoy of a mob
trampling on legitimate authority, a fact
which shows he cannot have any very friendly
leaning to the maintenance of this right.

Our London *working men will not be led
astray by what has been said as to the regula-
tions of provincial parks: For many reasons
the cases differ in their most essential
features. In the provincial towns largo
rooms for the purpose of holding popular
meetings can be easily obtained. In London
it is next to impossible to procure such places.
The prejudices or the fears of proprietors close
them, and where these do not operate, the ex-
pense of engaging thorn is so heavy that it
bars out the working classes almost altogether.
If Trafalgar-square or the Parks be shut, the
right of public meeting in the metropolis will
be practically at an end. The men in Parlia-
ment who are working for this object know
quite well what they are aiming at; and un-
less the public take up at once a firm atti-
tude, they will be successful, In the country,
too, it may be stated that the Parks are little
more than tastefully laid out promenades.
The field paths and hedge-rows are within
reach of the people on holiday e and Sundays;
whereas, the poor Londoner, unless he can find
his way into the Parks, with the right of free
recreation, has little chance of refreshing him-
self under those natural influences which in-
vigorate the body and refresh the spirit. Mr.
ArnToir, not. long ago, put himself before the
world as a kind of shabby genteel Tribune of
the people. At the present moment, in his
robes of office, he moves gracefully through a
Court minuet, to the delight of those lofty
and respectable persons whom he is seeking
to protect from the discomforting intrusions of
dusky radicals.

But, under all circumstances, and for rea-
sons innumerable, every privilege conneoted
with public parks, gardens; and open spaces,
should be insisted on strenuously; neither
Sovereigns, Prime Ministers, nor Commis-
sioners of Works should be allowed to abridge
popular rights, where the comfort, the health,
the pleasures and rights of the people are so
much at stake as they are in connexion with
our parks. To ()lose the London parks to
public gatherings would be to stifle the pub-
lic vnioo on great public questions in the me-
tropolis. The small halls in London are of no
use, the large halls are inaccessible by expense,
Trafalgar-square and the parks closed against
the people, with the Press already inacces-
sible, no adequate expression could be given
to the opinions of our metropolitan opera-
tives. And if we remember that within the
last ten years—nay, during any number of

past years—nearly every sound political
measure has found its most efficient support
from the working men gathering together in
their tens of thousands in the metropolis, we
may estimate pretty correctly how much
would be lost should they be doomed to
silence and inactivity by the devices of Govern-
ment officials, backed up by a House of
Commons professedly Liberal, but really in-
different in regard to some of the most
important requirements of the people. It is
true that Rotten-row and the Hyde-park
drive are very pretty as spectacles, but when
we remember that the people who enjoy them
have their own parks and country houses, and,
upon the whole enjoy life tolerably well as
spectators and actors in its various shows,
some little latitude might be given to those
poor people whose possessions are very limited,
and whose struggles for the light of heaven
or the light of liberty, have usually to be
carried on under many disadvantages and.dis-
couragements.

INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION.

IT is now nearly ten years ago since I pub-
lished a pamphlet entitled the "Reduction of
Taxation and the European Armaments and
Expenditure." The advocacy of this question,
or the dissemination of sound views upon it,
made but little progress for some time, when
it was suggested that a Congress should be
held in Geneva, which accordingly took place,
and was presided over by General GARI-
BALDI. I need not go into the causes of the
failure of that Congress, ; it is enough for us to
know that little or nothing came mit oft,
and that the cause languished, a few men in

keeping the matter olive. Later the Congress

an• address be presented to her MAJESTY,

caused men to look for some means to avert the
dire calamities of war, I knovv not, but it is

satisfactory to know that we can be heard now

nations bylnternationalArbitration with respect
and attention, instead of being considered
visionaries and impracticable enthusiasts. I
confess that when I and s ,me of my
English
friends left the Peace Congress at Geneva we
had very little hope that a Convention would
ever meet in that city to settle any dispute
that might arise between this country and
America, and although the proposed arbitra-
tion does not rem very promising at present
in consequence of the supposed exorbitant
demands of our trans-Atlantic friends, that
cannot in any way affect the great principle of
International Arbitration when it becomes
founded upon the compact of nations and based
upon a clear and well defined International
code. The statesmen of both countries would
do well to consider what the result would bccf. .

nary war on the Alabama question, instead of
submitting it to arbitration. To say nothing

countries, and, viewing such a conflict
only as a huge instrument for destroying
human life and wasting away of immeasurable
treasure, it becomes almost too frightful to
contemplate. The deplorable and humiliating

ment of an interregnum of fresh preparations
and the recruiting of strength to imminence
again a more gigantic saturnalia of blood and

Now, if history is worth anything, it
proves that those who were at the head of •

both of this and other countries to urge upen
their respective Governments the absolute
necessity for the mutual reduction of their
vast armaments, and the future settlement Of
all matters in dispute by arbitration, The
people of this country have now an excellent
opportunity of giving expression to their wishes
and desires in this respect, by pouring in
petitions to the 'louse of Commons in aupport
of Mr. IllcuuP's resolution praying that the
QUEEN will instruct her. Foreign Minister to
enter into negotiations with Foreign Govern-
ments with a view to the establishment of

national Arbitration.

We may rest assured that unless the matter
be forced upon the attention both of the
Government and Parliament of this country to
take tho initiative in this question in the
manner indicated by Mr. IticilAnn's motion, it
will never be done.

The working men, more than either the mid-
dle and upper planes, have a direct interest:to
causing a peaceful settlement of all matters
dispute between England and other countries'
They have to do nearly all the fighting and
find nearly all the money to carry on wars whinh
they have nothing to do with in originating:
The working men have to pay the greater par''
of the 423,000,030 a year interest upon the

ments over which they had no control. More-
over, the working men are now called uPOII

of marauding capitalists, and the negligenol
and connivance of the Foreign Minister of tile

nation. And not. only that, but these same
ers
unscrupulous political and mercantile gambl

WNES INSPECTION ACT.

Fon some years the course of legislation has
gone directly contrary to what the so-called
"principles of political economy " taught to
be the proper thing. The right of individual
enterprise to do the best it could for itself in
the freedom of trade—buying labour cheap,
and selling goods dear—had resulted in a
condition of things which could not have
endured much longer. In the accumulation
of wealth, the economy of humanity itself
appeared entirely forgotten. Children were
worked and sacrificed in factories, and men,
women, and children, in mines for hours, and
under circumstances of horror and evil never
exceeded in the annals of history. In 1831-2
the Factories Bill, and the Mines Inspection
Acts, broke into that system of cruelty, and
legal murder, which had been induced, we will
admit unintentionally, by the competition of
wealth against humanity, man against man,
and masters against each other. The em-
ployers of labour as a class; and the disciples
of the hard and fast economic school opposed all
such legislation. as contrary to the principles
of political economy, as subversive of the
freedom of trader the liberty of the subject,
and as dangerous to our national progress and
all interests of trade and commerce. And
against these protests these Acts passed—
while they looked on, we believe, with fear
and trembling—expecting to see England's
supremacy of trade upset, its wealth diminish ed ,
its manufactures ruined, and its workers de-
moralised. But, strange to say, the evils they
prophesied did not come to pass. Nay, it was
passing Strange that the very reverse followed.
From the time of passing these Acts, production
has inot:eased, trade has extended, capital
has aocumulated, and the workers have had a
decided advance in material benefits, and as de-
cided an elevation, both mental and moral. Had
the Factories Act not passed, had the impend-
ing revolution then looming been tided over,
it would have been impossible to have obtained,
and impolitic to have seized, the present
political suffrages, now quietly worked and
advantageously enjoyed, for the national
progress, by the great mass of the people.

Various improvements of the said acts in
favour of the workers, and, strange to say,
not to the ruin or even injury of the em-
ployers, have from time to time been introduced,
and at last, after years of delay, a real and
substantial measure of improvement has been
introduced in favour of the mines—in the
shape of the new Mines Regulation Bill,

The Aow Bill--under the heads of employ-
ment of women, young perilous, and children;
wages; workbag, managers, inspection, arbi-
tration; general, special, and miscellaneous
rules to be enforced by penalties—is conceived
and arranged under a mode and spirit very
different to what the old agitators and
workers of the previous Acts will well re-
member. Whereas it used to be, that the
promoters of the Inspection Acts and of its
improvement used to be treated as demagogues
and dangerous innovators; and whereas the
tendeney of what they advocated, and the bear-
ing of the things they sought for, were thought
to be illegitimate to economic philosophy, and
dangerous to the prosperity of the raining invest-
ments, thanks to the effort and conduct of the
Miners' Union and delegates; thanks to the
spirit of the age, and the beneficial results of
former experience; and oh, sad to think of it,
thanks to the constant horrible and wholesale
slaughter of the hundreds on occasion, and thou-
sands of known preventtble deaths of the poor
miners annually. A change has come over the
spirit of the dream of even Mr. Secretary
BRUCE. The miners are now considered to be
human men, whose lives and limbs are
actually of importance to the State, and
now their safety and their welfare, both
bodily and social, are actually considered
as equal to, if not positively before, the consi-
deration of coal—capital and coal. And now we
have the remonstrances of the miners' delegates
listened to, the miners' conferences and recom-
mendations heard, and their prayers and

petitions, in many important respects conceded
and provided formn the new Bill. During the
struggle for the last Inspections Act—in
1859-60—the miners had their delegates in
London working night and day for a limit to

_
the ages of boys being employed in the pits,
and for their hours of employment and educa-
tion. They asked for adequate protection of
life and limb in working and machinerk,
for compensation against neglect, when
lamed or killed, for a fair system of weighing
and valuing their work, for an ifficien4 in-
spection to secure adequate ventilation, so as
to do away with the clangors of explosion and
working, and for such measures of penalty and
punishment as might prove adequate to correct,
and just to enforce, in relation to both em-
ployers and employed, managers and men.
The delegates printed and provided a Bill to
effect what they sought, and the masters, in
opposition, prepared and provided a Bill to
seoure what they thought best for themselves.
We would that the two were now printed side
by side, to give evidence and illustration of
the wisdom and humanity of the two classes.
The bill prepared by the employers left out
the education of the young and time of work-
ing, it left out all relating to weighing and
valuing coal for the men, it opposed equal and
adequate penalties, increased inspection, and
further provision for safety. And the Go-
vernment, like a vessel pulled by two opposite
forces, attempted to sail betwixt a.nd between,
but ultimately gave way to the stronger cord
pulling—capital; being many of themselves

personally and pecuniarily interested ; and

they gave all they could for the interests of
capital, and as little as they dared
for the benefit of the men. And it
followed thus that all positive provi-
sions for education were avoided; the
time too long for years too early to sus-
tain for boys gsing into the pits, was granted;
the work of women on the pit banks was un-
restricted; truck permitted in many districts ;
the old and inadequate system of inspection
continued; so that the evil was not attended
to until after accidents or explosions had
occurred, and then it was to be duly reported
upon. Prevention was not attempted, nor
compensation provided for when neglect was
proved; nor was an adequate fine for the
principal fixed, and while the worker might
be imprisoned, the master escaped by, to him,
a trilling fine, and from imprisonment, however
deserved, he was exempt. And lastly, while
the men were, at their own cost, at liberty to
appoint a check-weigher, to see they had fair
weight registered, the cwts. per ton were not
fixed, and so custom might legalise any
weight, and by way of a rider the men were
' restricted to a certain clas a of cheek men
which the Masters could, and often did, nega-
tive, by discharging them. Altogether, the
Act was partial„ one-sided, and inadequate to
Bemire either security for life or limb to the
worker, or satisfaction :as to the justice or
judgment of the managers. Tho young were
neglected, and the old unprotected; the
inspection a farce as a preventitive„and a folly.
as a check to the evils which told first upon
the men, an ultimately upon the masters
themselves. And now as to the changes and
improvements in the new Bill :--

1. Children are still to be introduced into
mines at ten years of age (the men ask for
12), but the time for working is restricted to 6
hours a day, if employed more than three days
in any one week, and not more than 10 hours
in any one day. No male or young person
above 13 and under 16, shall be employed in
any mine more than 66 hours in any week,
with certain provided exceptions. The em-
ployment of women is still net forbidden, but
it is regulated by the Workshops Ad.
2. Education is positively provided for and
enforced by attendance at a certified school,
betwixt the ages of ten and thirteen, when
employed in mines of not less than twenty
hours a week. The enforcement to be by the
employer, or parents, or guardians, and the
teacher is to be paid by deducting the neces-
sary fees from the wages of the boy in question.
All this is to be regulated by certificates, and
we trust the inspector will be arranged for so i
as to inspect them. -

3' Wages."--All wages are to be paid for en
fnoney, and not at any public-house, beershop,

or place of entertainment, where intoxicating
liquor is sold; and if " truok " be attempted,
a penalty may be duly enforced.
4. As a rule the workmen are to be paid by-
the weight of coals they get, for, as a rule, the
coals are sold by weight to the consumer.
Still, the SECRETARY of STATE may allow ex-
ceptions, if expedient, though we confess
ignorance of why they should be. And to
secure fair weight, the legal standard of 20
cwt. per ton is fixed, as by Act 5 and 6 of
WIT,LIA3I IV., and Act 5 of her present
MAJESTY. The men may also appoint any

agent at their own cost, to see and register
the weights charged to each man, so that
justice may be rendered satisfactory, and that
' the men.'s agent shall have adequate facilities
granted without dispute, so long as he does not
interfere with the proper and peaceful working
of the mine, This is an immense boon to the,
miners, as we could show in the history of how
they have been cheated in weight, and dodged,
and defeated at the cost of thousands when
they attempted to put check- weighmen.
5. Provisions for safety and better ventila-
tion are to:be scoured by additional shafts, and
superior arrangements. And thus the Hartley
Pit catastrophes may in future be avoided.
6. For the first time, though long sought for
by the men, the managers of mines are to be
subjected to an examination to test their
efficiency, and to be certificated, as to ability,
character, and conduct. Examinations to be
appointed by the SECAEIAILY Of STATE, and to
be certified accordingly; the certificate to be
forfeited, or penalties enforced in oases of
neglect, incompetency, or drunkenness, proved
after pliblic enquiry.
7. Inspectors to be provided, As hitherto,
with all past powers and duties; and with
the additional ones Of reporting and enforcing
all the provisions of the new Act. But, unless
the staff of inspectors be increased, it vill be
radically impossible for them to do their duty,

however willing. This is, however, left to the
discretion of the SECRETIRY Of STATE; who
may or may not exercise it well and wisely;
or he may restrict and economise to the loss
. of both lives and the public weal.
8. The regulations relating to coroners and
juries remain much as before, and so do many
of the conditions of the general rules. Others
are, however, changed and addeit to for the
better. Among other things in; the special
rules, fifteen enforces withdrawal of the work-
ing men in case Of danger. Now we happen
to remember the ease of men in a mine, at
Barnsley, not warned. The owner had nine
horses drawn up, when the explosion anti-
cipated warred, and some seventy men were
destroyed by it. There was no rule ordering
notice of danger, and so the poor fellows lest
their lives. The Union, however, made him.
pay some compensation—about the price of a
horse—which he did quietly, rather than risk
' a trial. Other arrangements for safety, and
especially for blasting by gunpowder, are laid
down, which are likely to prove beneficial. The
28th special rule is new entirely. It states
that if the persons employed in a mine are
dissatisfied with the security of any
part of it, they may, at their own cost, send
two persons to inspect its arrangements,
and for which facility should be allowed by
the managers. And their report, signed by
them, shall be entered in a book to be kept for
that purpose. Now this we believe to be an
excellent provision, for in many instances we
know that the men have protested against the
danger, and have been unnoticed or unheeded.
But while this may be good in intention, we
' see great difficulty in the men carrying it out.
It is to be at their own Cost, and that involves
the difficulty in getting any considerable
number to incur that cost. The danger may
be local, a few only may know of it, and they
could not, or would not, afford to pay coin-
petent.examiners. Competent examiners must
be practical men, and if workmen, employed
either at that mine or in others near, they
would be liable to be pecked at and discharged
should they make a report unfavourable,
however true. The pit owners will be sure to
band themselves together to protect their
interests, and they will, of course, peek at
men whose proceedings they think to be ob-
jectionable to their class. This, and other
provisions of the Act, will render the trades

unions of the men desirable, if not impera-
lively necessary; for, singly, the men will
not be able to work it, and unity for good is
not quite so easy as some people thiak it to be
for what they say is evil. And this too in-
volves difficulty, but we hope not irreme-
diable. Good is not-very easily attained at any
time, and we are not disposed to be cast down
easily.

9. Besides general rules, there are to be
especial
such as WO necessary for theconditionof each mine. And these
s pe o
airile
to be legal must first be posted up a fortaight
at the pit, and then trnnsmitted, to the
Inspector and SICRETA.RY of STATE. And Whilt
is new is, that objections are also to be
received from any of the workers, to
be entertained and considered by the Itispeotor
and SECRETARY of STATE, and noticed to the
owners of the mines, and if arranged for satis-
factorily, the special rules are to be legalised ;
if not, they are to be referred to a court for
consideration, and so accepted on rejected in
favour of both.

Such are the principal heads of the Act and
the character of the changes preferred under
the head, penalties.

10. After the courts for trying offenoss
have been arranged, we have the penal-
ties regulated, that the owner himself
may be" sued, as well as deputy (who aught
be worth nothing), and the penalties are made
more fitting to the relative positions and means
of men and masters; and what is. still more
significant and just, is, that the owner as well
as employed, may be imprisoned, with or
without hard labour, for not exceeding time
months, "in ease of gross neglect," or "when
the court is of opiniona pecuniary penalty will
not meet the circumstances of the case."
, Hitherto the owper could escape, while the
Worker could be and was sent to prison. Of
course we do not think that this improved Act
will work perfectly or meet every c Lae.. We
see difficulties in working, and particularly in
authorities and courts. We can understand
that the SECRETARIES Of STATE, inspectors, and
officials will see their own way and lean man-
rally to their own class interests. But what
we rejoice to see, is, throughout', the intention
to protect and to benefit the worker, and to do
justice to humanity as well as to wealth. MitY
it succeed; and to that intent we urge upon the
miners and their National Ezeoutivo to du their
best to carry the whole Bill, with snob ahem.,
Cons and additions as we purpose to refer to
again; but they must act promptly, or their
opponents will be to much for SOON of (ho
best clauses and provisions.

The adjourned meeting of agrieultur4 labourers

was held at the Prince of Wales Inn, Hagley, on
Monday night. Mr. T. Hunt occupied the chair,
and there was a largo attendance. It was reported
that several farmers in the parishes of Pedmoro,
Hagley, Clent, Kinver, and Cookie), had given
the rise, 2s. 6d., as required, for labourers, and 18s.
per week to wagoners, in some places with Per-
quisites and in other places the beer was taken
off, and the men had continued work. Some
farmers in other parishes had given the rise in
certain cases, is., and other cases 25., and some
men had struck in consequence
.of the masters
refusing to give them an increase. A number a
speeches were delivered, and it was proposed and
carried unanimously, "That they should continue
to agitate until the rest of the men had obtained
the rise asked for." It was stated that in some
instances the farmers had offered the rise to some
of the men and not to others, and it was resolved
that unless all the men receive the advance that
the men at each farm should strike until the whole
of the men should have the increase.

THE RENEWED AGITATION AMONG COLLIERS.
numerously attended meeting of miners was
held on Tuesday night, at the Shakespeare Inn,
Xow Mill-street. Mr. Levi Brittain presided, and it
was unanimously resolved to give notice on the
22nd of March unless the benefits of the nine
hours system are conceded to the bandsmen, and a
sixth was taken off the stints of pikemen. .It was
also decided that a levy should be made through-
out the district in support of the agitation.
Attention was called to the Hartley Fund
balance, and it was resolved to hold a conference
respecting the matter on Easter Monday.

FLAX, AND WOOLLEN TRADES.

On Saturday afternoon a crowded meeting of the
operatives employed in the felt, flax, and woollen
trades of Leeds and the district was held in the
Assembly-rooms, to take into consideration the

_
nine hours movement for women and children
working in the factories, It had been intended to
have a demonstration on Woodhouse Moor, but
there was such a drenching rain that this arrange-
ment could ,not be carried out. Great numbers
gathered in the neighbourhood of the Assembly-
rooms, both before and after tho meeting, and
during a brief improvetnent in the weather there
was a procession, headed by a band of music.
The oper,ttives are apparently bent on taking
active steps to secure the object they have in
view.

Recently they sent out a circular addressed "to
. ,
the mast( r flax and silk spinners, felting and
woollen manufacturers of Leeds and districts," in
which they said
"We, the operatives working in the above
factories, thank you sincerely for the hour and a
half given to us a short time ago, and we earnestly
but most rospectfully request that you will make a
further concession of four and a half hours, viz.,
nitile per day. Fifty-four to constitute a week, to
commence on the first of March, and that, the
following be our working time : —Monday, Tuesday,
Wednesday, Thursday, from six in the morning to
five in the. ,afternoon ; Friday, from six in the
morning to half-past five in the afternoon; Satur-
day, from six in the Morning to half-past twelve
at noon, without any reduction of wages; and
where any of us are paid by the piece, we ask that
you will advance ,our. priees in proportion to the
redirced hours in order that we Inv be able to earn
the samaaraount of wages. We ask for this conces-
sion because that we think that our work is as irk-
some and laborious as any other; wo have to be
very attentive and watchful while at work ; also
considering the pernicious Lind 'hurtful nature of
our department. We beg to call your attention to
all others who are now working only nine hours
per day, who are nearly all adult males, while 'the
largest portion by far working in factories are
women and children, who should not work any
longer, if as long. We a1.z.0 beg to call to your
notice the fact that the greatest portion of the

At the meeting on Saturday this circular was

hands and many overlookersi warmly applauded

The first resolution that was adopted declared

deep regret the indifference of their employers to
the great boon they are asking, namely, nine hours
for a day's work, without any reduction in wages,
and that the meeting pledge itself not to rest
satisfied until all men, women, and children have
obtained it. It was also the opinion of the meet-
ing, as expressed
,by the seeond resolution, that

ing in factories should have the nine hours system
granted to them, seeing that a great number of
other branches of business have obtained it already.
This concession they, asked of theim employers
because they think their work is laborious and
injurious to their health, while they have to be
attentive and watchful when at work. Seeing
also that the largest number of persons employed
in the factories are women and children, they
think it a great shame that they should have to
work ten hours a day, while able-bodied men are
working only nine hours a day. By the third
resolution it was declared to be desirable that the
meeting should pledge itself to send two delegates
from each firm to represent the respective opera-

League Committee. A.ll the resolutions vrere

THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

At a meeting of the operatives, hold at the
Temperance Hall, Walsall, on Monday night, the
following rules, which had been prepared by the
Committee appointed at the meeting on the 16th
inst., were produced and approved. It was stated
that a copy had been sent to the employers for
their approval. The rules were as follows :-
1. That the wages be Gid. per hour for fair
average workmen; but superior or inferior work-
men may be paid at such rate of wages as may be
decided by the employer or his foreman. 2. That the
hours of labour for the first,five days of the week
shall be from 6 a.m. to 6p.m., and on Saturdays
from 6 a.m. to 1 p.m. That all overtime be paid
at the rate of lid. per hour for ibe first two hours,
9d. for the next two hears, and all time after that till
six o'clock the next morning be-paid for as double
time. One hour shall be allowed for dinner and
half an hour for breakfast. 3. Men employed on
unprotected buildings during the winter months
shall work from light till dark, with one hour
only allowed for meals, and such time to be
reckoned as nine hours; but where the building is
protected, and artificial light is required, the
employer shall provide such. 4. That the em-
ployer shall commence the payment of wages
Within ten minutes after the time fixed for closing
Work on Saturdays; and in no ease shall wages be
paid in a 'public-house. 5. That all men sent to
na out•door job shall walk to their work in their
employers' time. No time to be allowed to the
'workmen for returning from work, except on Sa-
turdays, when each workman shall leave work at
such a time as will enable him to be at the pay-
table at 1.15 p.m. For all distances exceeding
four miles, a sufficient sum for lodgings, time,
travelling expenses to and from the place of work,
shall be paid by the employer to the workmen.
6. That where a number of men are employed on
the same piece of work, instructions shall be given
to them through the foreman appointed to take
the lead by the employer. 7. All men must give
and take a week's notice—such notice to expire at
the close of the day's work, but in oases of
drunkenness or neglect of work, any workman
may be discharged without notice. 8. That these
rules shall come into operation on the 6th of May,
1872. 9. That a printed copy of these rules shall
be posted by the masters in some conspicuous
place in each workshop.

articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

Pr. Aubery George Spencer, Bishop of
Jamaica, who has been a resident at Torquay
for some time past, died on Saturday morning.
The deceased prelate, who was formerly of
Magdalen Hall, Oxford, was consecrated to the
bishopric of Newfoundland in 1839, and trans-
lated to the see of Jamaica in 1843. Dr.
Spencer was seventy-seven years of age.

The Navy Estimates, which were issued on
Slturday, show that the total sum required
t 92. the Current year is £9,508,149, a decrease
ns (.ortipared with last year of £281,807. 1.1-. a
i'ems in which the largest increase occurs are
ri avid stores, victuals, and clothing, dockyards,
and Admiralty Office. The decrease is in
"steam machinery anti ships built by contract,
new works and buildings, and wages to seaman
and marines.

Preparations for a demonstration against the
ltoyal Parks and Gardens Bill are being made
for Sunday next, in Hyde-park.

Considerable excitement appears to prevail
in Antwerp owing to the movement which is
going On there in connection with the Comte
do Chambord. A notica has been issued by
the municipal authorities prohibiting any
assemblage of more than five persons in the
streets. The Mayor of Antwerp, in another
proclamation, has called upon all citizens who
are friends of order "not to encourage by their
presence manifestations which can only preju-
dice the honour and reputation of the city."
So great, nevertheless, was the excitement on
Saturday night, that the Comte de Chambord's
hotel had to be surrounded by gendarmes, and
all traffic in the street was prohibited.

M. Thiers has, it is said, informed a Cathoiie
member that, in consequence of the represen-
tations of Italy, the French Government will
shortly appoint an ambassador to Rome.

There is likely to be a very animated debate
in the French Assembly on the Bill brought
forward by the Government to protect itself
against attacks in the press. M. Gambetta
ha i defended the Bill in one of the Committees,
and M. Jules Simon has declared that if it
should not pass he will resign.

M. Grelier, who was ut one time Minister of
the Interior under the Commune, has just been
arrested at Mendon, in the house of the Jesuit
Fathers, where he has for many months been
working as a cook.

The polling for the, Wick Burghs, which
took place on Saturday, resulted in the return
of Mr. Pander by a majority of 206 votes over
Ur. Reid.

Mr. Stanley Vickers N.P. for Wallingford,
died on Saturday at the early ago of thirty-
five. The deceastd gentleman, who was a
partner in the firm of Joseph and John
'Vickers, distillers, was returned for Walling-
ford at the general election of 1808.

In the Court of Exchequer on Saturday a
young woman named Watkins, a dressmaker,
obtained £320 damages against Mr, William
Rainey, a negro, and an English barrister, for
a bteach of promise of marriage,

On Saturday the Court of Exchequer.
chamber in Dublin delivered judgment in
the ease of the Hertford estates, on an
appeal from a decision of the Court of Com-
mon Pleas. The result is that the estates
of the late Marquis of Hertford go to Sir.
Richard Wallace, and not to Sir Hamilton
Seymour.

The February sessions of the Central Cri-
minal Court were opened on Monday.

The remains of Ueorge Merritt, who wa
last week murdered in the Belvedere-road
Lambeth, were on Tuesday interred in Tooting,
Cemetery. A large number of Foresters, an
order to which the deceased belonged, joined
in the funeral procession.

Mr. B rues, on Monday, in replying to adepu-
tation introdueed by Lord Abinger' promised
that, without pledging himself to all the
details of Mr. Dillwyn's Salmon Fisheries Bill,
the Government would give it their active
support.

The official declaration of the polling at the
North Notts election was made -on Monday.
vvheu thp High Sheriff announced that 2,680
votes had been recorded for Mr. Nlonckton,
and 1,624 tor Mr. Layeock, thus giving a
Conservative majority of 1,050.

At Monday's sitting of the Central Criminal
Court, an application was made for a bill of
indictment at common law against the Lord
A.dvaQate of Sootland for the alleged offence of
not, in his official capacity, proceeding against
one of the Scotch judges tor an infraction of
Jaw. The Deputy-Recorder declined to inter-
fere, on the ground that he had no
jurisdiction.

William 'Chester Minor, who is charged with
the wilful murder of George Merritt in Bel-
vedere-road, Lambeth, has been again brought
Up at the Southwark Police-court, and com-
naitted for trial.

Comments upon the Alabama
_question con-
tinue to appear in the New York papers.
The World now says it is no wonaer Great
Britain objects to the indirect claims being
submitted to the arbitrators, as her financial
life would thus be placed in their hands for
the next quarter of a century. The Washington
correspondent of the fleraN declares that the
United States Government is willing to accept
a round sum of ten millions sterling for the
Alabama damages, and has authorised several
bankers to informally communicate this to the
British Government.

Lord Lyons attended the thanksgiving
service in the Rue d'Aguesseau, Paris, on
Tuesday. The church was very full. This
was also the case in the Avenue Marbeuf, not-
withstanding that many English residents
had gone to London to witness the ceremonies
there.

The Governor of 'Bombay, and all the Go-
vernment officials attended in state a special
Thanksgiving Service at the Cathedral for the
recovery of H.R.R. the Prince of Wales.
The Gackwar has.placed a lac of rupees at the
Governor's disposal for a public work in
honour of the event. The Honourable Bassoon
has added 5,000 rupees to his former contribu-
tion of a lao of rupees for a new high school,
as a Thanksgiving offering. The Parsees,
invited by Sir Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoi, met at
the Fire Temple, and the Jewish community,
at the request of the Honourable Sassoon' held
a solemn service in their synagogue. At the
invitation of the Hfnourable Munguldass Na-
thoobhoti about 10,000 Bombay Hindoos of
all denominations assembled in the Mom-
badabee Temple, and offered up thanksgivings.
Similar meetings were held by Mahomedans
and every soot of undoes.

A holiday was observed at Calcutta as a
mark of rejoicing on the recovery of the Prince
of Wales; and Thanksgiving Services have
been held in all the churches and chapels.

The following resolutions were passed the
other night at the meeting of the Council of
the Marylebone Electoral Reform Association,
at their rooms, Waterloo Arms, High-street,
Marylebone :—" That this Council learns with
deep regret that the Government has omitted
from the Ballot Bill of this session the clause
that provides for the payment of the necessary
election expenses by the ratepayers, and trusts
that immediate steps will be taken to rectify
the omission that so injuriously affects those
candidate's who, although possessed of every
other qualification, are not itufficiently
wealthy to pay the present enormous de—
mands.' 2. " That this Council acknow-
ledge the letter of J. H. Lewis, Esq., M.P.,
and thanks him for his continued resistance
to the Royal Parks and Gardens Bill; and
also for the services rendered by the Bill
before Parliament for a reform in the regis-
tration of voters."

The Committee, consisting of Lord Dal-
housie, Sir George Grey, and Mr. Mansell,
who vere appointed to inquire into Sunday
labour at the Post-offiee, have presented their
report to Parliament. They are of opinion
that there should be made more favourable
conditions for the discontinuance of a Sunday,
post. They propose that a Sunday rural post
shall be taken oil if the receivers Of two-thirds
of the letters for the district desire its dis-
continuance, and that no Sunday rural post
shall be pat on unless the receivers of two-
thirds of the letters for the district desire its
establishment, or (as the case may be) its re-
storation. They think that the practice of
making a Sunday delivery to callers at the
Post-oflioe, in place of a house delivery, is
objectionable. They suggest that the work of
collection on Sunday be restricted.

On Monday night, in the large hall of the
Bow and Bromley Institute, Mr. R. W. John-
ston, of the Postal Telegraph Department,
delivered his popular lecture on the "Elect
Telegraph" to nearly 1,000 persons. The
lecture was illustrated by specimens of all the
instruments in use in the postal system,
including a working model of the pneumatic
tube; and the hall was placed en rapport with
Liverpool and Edinburgh, with which towns
messages were exchanged. The conclusion of
the lecture, in which reference was made to
the part played by the teletr''raph during the
illness of the Prince of Wales, was received
with great applause.

Two girls residing at Crook, near Wigan,
wipe drowned on Saturday morning in the
Leeds .and Liverpool Canal. They worked at
one of the Wigan factories, and their nearest
way to the mill lay along the towing path of
the canal, It is supposed that in turning a
corner one of the girls was blown into the
water, and that the other lost her life in
attempting to rescue her companion.:

It ig stated that the visit of the Prince of
Wales to Yarmouth will not be of so long a
duration as was at first anticipated. In a
letter to Lord Suffield, his Royal Highness
has expressed his regret that in consequence
of his going abroad he will be obliged to cur-
tail his visit to two or three days, and states
that in connection with his visit to Norfolk
he will have to be present at the Agricultural
Show at Lynn, which is to be held in June.

On Saturday, the Queen held a Court at
Windsor Castle, and received addresses of
congratulation from the Corporation of London,
and from the City Commission of Lieutenancy,
on the occasion of the recovery of the Prince
of Wales. After the ceremony, the Lord
Mayor, with Mr. R. N. Philips, M.P. Alder-
man Lawrence M.P., Mr. C. Reed, NIP., and
Mr. Ambrose Lawrence,
the movers and seconders
of the respeotive addresses, wore presented to
her Majesty.

At the Assize Court of Rouen, the trial has
taken place of M. Janvier de la Motto, Pre-
fect of the Eure under the Imperial Govern-
ment, who is mused of embezzlement and
forgery. The court was thronged with the
most distinguished people of the Departments
of the Seine Inferieure and the Eure. M.
Lattehand, the famous criminal lawyer, is conn-
sel for the accused. The indictment alleges
that M. Janvier de la Motto led a most im-
moral life, which at last became so shameless.
that his wife was compelled to obtain a sepa-
ration from him. It states that he was over-
whelmed with debts, and that in the year
1868, no fewer than 140 writs were issued
against him for an aggregate sum of 296,582
francs. The specific charges against him are
very numerous. He is accused of falsifying
his accounts, and of appropriating to his own
purpose the public money which passed
through his hands, His alleged frauds ex-
tend over a period of ten years, and are said to
reach to an enormous amount. His statement,
.by way of defence, is, that large surns of
money were entrusted to him, and that in dis-
bursing them he confided in the honesty of
others, and did not keep good accounts. He
admitted that his private life was not free
from reproach. The trial is not yet concluded.

Earl Granville has received a telegram from
the British Vice-Consul at Damascus stating
that certain English travellers who were made
prisoners at Kerak have been liberated.

The Deutscher Turnverein, or German Gym-
nastic Society, hold its annual carnival on
Tuesday night, at the Society's Hall, in Old
St. Pancras-road. A ball, which was largely
attended by the members and their friends,
was commenced about 9 o'clock, and dancing
was kept up with great spirit until a late
hour.

Lord Edward Bulwer Lytton has replied to
tho Committee of the Conservative Students,
and, as anticipated, refuses to aceept the office
of Lord 'teeter, which had fallen to him in
consequence of his opponent, Mr. Ruskin,
being ineligible, in the terms of the Scottish
University Act.

The Cunard steamer Parthia, whilst pro-
ceeding to sea from Liverpool to Boston, came
into collision with the screw steamer Emiliano,
inward bound, from Singapore and Manilla.
The Emiliano had to be beached near Tran-
mere, and her cargo consisting of sugar and
tobacco, will •be almost destroyed. After
striking the Erailiano the Parthia ran lute the
steamer Nina, bound from Vigo, doing her
considerable damage. The Partina is so much
damaged that she will be unable to proceed
to sea for a few days. Fortunately, with the
exception of some trifling hurts, no serious
personal damages took place.

The Pope has addressed a letter to the
French Bishops, in which he urges them to
exert their influence on behalf of the Comt de
Chatnbercl.

A Berlin correspondent says that at present
it is doubtful whether an attempt on Prince
Bismarck's life was seriously intended by the
young man from Posen who has just been
arrested in the Prussian capital. It seems
that the pistol he had with him when taken
into custody has been in his possession for
years—ever since he served in the Papal
2ouaves,—and that it wus a letter of his
foster-mother which brought him to Berlin.

At the English chapel in Berlin a service
was celebrated to return thanks for the re-
covery of the Prince of Wales.

The Empercr of Austria has written a letter
to the Pope, stating that the presence of his
Holiness is required near Germany, in order
that be may combat the schism now taking
place in that country. It is probable that
Pius IX. will leave Rome before Easter.

At the Marlborough-street Polioe Court on
Wednesday a professor of swimming was
convicted of an assault upon a city merchant
and ids clerk, and was sentenced to a month's
imprisonment in each case.

A private letter from Zanzibar, of the 7th
January, describes an interview which the
American Consul and several American mer-
chants resident there had had on tho previous
night with the Sultan (Sieet Bonyoush). His
Royal Highness was about to start on a pil•
grirnar,oe for Mecca, and he assured his visitors
that the messengers sent by him- some tine
ago on the track of Mr. Stanley, OS New
York. Herald correspondent would be back
within twenty days at farthest. They are ex-
pected to bring news from Mr. Stanley, and
possibly some definite intelligence about Dr.
Livingstone.
A rumour prevails in Brussels that the
Communist leaders, Raoul Rigault, and Gene-
ral Cluseret, are at Geneva, preparing ani.
insurrectional movement in the south -
France.

4111 An official announcement has been issue
by the police at Leipzig, prohibiting tile
enrolment of members of the Internatlon!!l
Society, on the ground of its demoorau°
objects.

General Sherman and President Grant's son
have visited Pompeii. Some special excail-
tions were made during their stay.

News from the Looshai expedition is to the
20th inst. General Bourchter telegraphs that
the whole of the country through which he
has passed is now subdued. Three chiefs of
one of the tubes have been sent as hostageh
and a fine has been paid.

Immense crowds again thronged the prin-
cipal streets of London on Wednesday tl°
witness the remnants of the decorations an'
of the illuminated devices. In the evening
the vehicular traffic added considerably to the
dangers of the curious multitudes who were
compelled by the pressure to turn off fro'
the pavements into the roadways.

Mr. It. S. Rolford, the senior Conservative
member for East Gloucestershire, is, in conse-
quence of ill health, about to resign the seat
which he has held. for eighteen years. Mt.
Reginald Yorke, a former member for Tewkes..
bury, is expected to offer himself as a candi-
date.

M. Thiers, it is rumoured in Paris, intends
to raise the state of siege there during April.

A telegram from Rome announces that the
Pope is receiving a large number of addresses
from religious bodies' urging him to abandon
his idea of leaving. that city.

I correspondent at Antwerp says that that
town has at once resumed its ordinary gate
now that the Comte de Chambord has gone
away to Holland. The people were, it seem•
s,
divided into two parties—one for, and the
other against the Count. The former party
consisted of the petty traders and the poorer,
classes ; the latter, of the wealthier class 0'
merchants and traders of all kinds, as well AS
the people employed by them. The Count ltas
departed not a day too soon, as far as We
business interests of Antwerp are coneernedt
inasmuch as one of the four great wool fain)
of the year conimeneed there on Tuesday. '

Mr. Justice Hannen on Wednesday admitted '
to bail Mr. Edmonds, who has been committed
for trial for the alleged murder of kis wile'
His Lordship ordered Mr. Edmonds to "1,,(3
security, himself in £4,000, und to
sureties for the same amount.

Prince Ladislas Czartoryski and his wife, the
Princess Marguerite de Nemours gave, on Mos'
day, at the Hotel Lambert, a grand soiree osuli
posed exclusively of Poles. The cards °.
invitation were drawn up in the nativelangog"
of the host and his guests.

The number of perms employed in the
diamond fields of the Cape Colony is now
large, and the amount of their "finds r
enormous, compared with the yield from tue.

The Rev. A. S. Herring, incumbent of St'
Paul's, Clerkenwell, held it ehildrezeifthigillgl"
giving entertainment in Jus parish.

MARCH 2, 1872.

According to another Paris telegram, the
Powers which have commercial treaties with
France intend to remonstrate with the French
Government against the proposed tax on raw
materials.

Last week the aggregate mortality in
London and twenty other large towns in the
United Kingdom wds at the rate of 26 deaths
annually to every 1,000 persons estimated to
be living. In the metropolis 2,328 births and
• 1,488 .deaths were registered, the former
having been 117 and the latter 192 below the
average. Fifty-three persons died from
small-pox, 52 from measles, 32 from scarlet
fever, 2 from diphtheria, 97 from whooping-
cough, 32 from different forms of. fever (of
which 3 were certified as typhus' 15 as enteric
or typhoid, and 14 as simple continued fever),
and 8 from diarrlima. The temperature was
again considerably above the average through-
out the week.

On Wednesday the Master of the Rolls gave
judgment in an application by the official
liquidator of the Lundy granite Company for
an order requiring Mr. Harvey. 'Lewis, M.P.,
to refund £135, paid to him as a remuneration
for his Services as a director. The ground of
the application was that the directors were
not entitled to their fees' because the company
had made no profits. Mr. Lewis contended
that he had been properly paid under a proviso
in one of the articles, but Lord Romilly held
that the money must be refunded. •

The death is announced of the daughter of
Mungo Park, the celebrated African traveller.

Colonel William Burns, last surviving son
of Robert Burns, died at his residence at
Cheltenhamon Wednesday, aged eighty-one.

The journals kept by Sir John Burgoyne
during the campaigns of 1809-10-11-12-13
and 'l4, which have been discovered among his
papers, and also his private correspondence
during the Crimean War, are about to be pub-
lished.

On Saturday, Lord Kinnaird unveiled at
Dundee a statue which has just boon erected
to commemorate George Kinloch, of Kinloch,
who, in consequence of his advocacy of
political rights, was compelled to flee the
country nearly forty years ago.

The Admiralty have decided on abolish-
ing the training brigs for boys and
ordinary seamen at Portsmouth and Devon-
port, and one of the large frigates will be at
Once commissioned for the purpose of being
employed in teaching the seamen and 143
practical seamanship at sea.

The number of paupers in receipt of relief
at Manchester on the Ist ult. was—lndoor
3,113, outdoor 4,983, making a total of 8,09 G,
being a decrease of 5,000 on the cotre-
sponiling date of 1871; and a decrease also of
2,000 on the average number of paupers for the
previous six years.

The Irish Temporalities Commissioners
have decided on 3,063 out of 6,227 eominu-
tation claims, and have already paid over for
commutation annuities £4,000,000 sterling.
The bill Which is about to be introduced for
the modification of the Commiseion will pro.
Tide for the formation of a full Court of
Appeal. It will include a provision to enable
&judicial member of the Privy Council to sit
and hear appeals with the two Commissioners.

Master Gibson, one of the taxing officers in
.the Irish Court of Chancery, died suddenly
On Tuesday week in Dublin.

As a boat containing nine 'persOns *as
approaching Curraghniore, on Lough Musk,
touts" of Mayo, it was upset, and sit persons
drowned.

The Figeeoh Of the Attorney-General in the
Tiohborne case is the longest in any legal case
on record, and extended over twenty-five
days. Mist Sheddon spoke for twenty-four
days in the celebrated declaration of iegitimacy
ease, and Serjeant Wilde (afterwards Lord
Truro) spoke twelve days (three House of
Lards Weeks) in " Small v. Attwood." Sir
Charles Wetherell is also said to have spoken
for twenty days.

Thomas Bellamy Mears, at Bond's Patent
Brick Works; Birmingham, hdving slipped,
fell on his neck between two cog-wheels, which
severed his head from his body and also one of
his arms.

There is in the Chester workhouse a man
named David Powell, who fought and was
wounded in that remarkable action between
the Shannon and the Chesapeake during the
last war between England and the United
States.

A burglary has been effected At Argyll Ilan,
Torquay, the residence. of Lord Lytton. Some
valuable property Was carried off, and the
thieves litivc not boon traced.

Dr. Sohn Rose Cormack, upon whom her
Majesty has signified her intention of con-
ferring knighthood, in recognition of his set-
vices during the siege of Paris, and as a mili-
tary surgeon on the field and in the ambulances
through the late war, is now Physician to the
British Hospital at Paris, which bears the
name of the late Lord Hertford.

Lord Richard Grosvenor,' MP., has accepted
the office of Vice-Chamberlain, in the room of
Lord Castlerosse, called to the House of Peers.

In addition to the volunteer review at
Brighton on Easter Monday, another is to be
held at Portsmouth some time in April.

The Royal yacht Victoria and Albert is, it
is said, ordered to be got ready to proceed to
the Mediterranean about the middle of March,
for the service of the Prince of Wales,
who will, it is understood, at that date
visit Mentone or Nice. A residence near the
Wellington pier, at Great Yarmouth, is also
stated to have been selected as a temporary
residence for his Royal Highness during part
of May.

The Poet-Laureate has presented to the
Prime Minister a memorial, in which are set
forth the claims of Mr. R. IL Horne to be
allowed to participate in the pensions awarded
from the Civil List in recognition of literary,
scientific, and other public services. Among
Hr. Tennyson's co-signatories are Mr. Brown-
ing, Mr. Swinburne, Mr. Rossetti, Mr. Morris,
Mr. Matthew Arnold, Mr. Carlyle, Lor
Lytton, Sir Henry Taylor, Mr. .Ruskin,
Professor Owen, and Miss Harriet Martineau.

The South Loudon Press says that the
seat for East Surrey cost Mr. Watney 6,0081.
2s. 2d. His opponent only spent half that
sum.

Mr. Ruskin has given up his house at
Denmark-hill, and has bought a small estate
at Coniston Lake, where he intends to reside,
dividing his time between Coniston, Oxford,
and the Continent.

The Temps announced erroneoul.ly that
Colonel Denfort was elected to the Protestant
Consistory against M. Guizot. The figures
are :—Gmzot, 1,003; Denfert, 975.

The grand Parliament of the Gipsies, which
meets every seven years, has just assembled
in the pretty town of Cannstatt, on the
Neckar, near Stuttgardt, It is at present
presided over by King Joseph Reinhardt, an
old man of 98, Delegates have arrived from
all countries—England, Spain, Rus' sia ao..
They deliberate on the common interests of
those nomad tribes, found in every habitable
part of theglobe. A vast number of foreigners
have flocked to Wurtemberg to witness the
Various ceremonies, which are rendered more
curious by the infinite variety of the costumes.

Herr Wolff, a Dntch author, has discovered
a copy of Jacob van iklaerlant's " Trojan War,"
whieh appears to be nearly, it not quite,
complete. Hitherto, only 8,000 lines of this
thirteenth century poem have been known,
but the new manuscript oontainkabout 88,400
lines.

The demand for sittings in the Rev. Henry
Ward Beecher' s church being very great,
many of the pewholders have agreed to under
let their pews for the evening service. Nr.
Beecher has publicly expressed his approval
of this; observing from the pulpit:—" One
sermon carefully listened to is enough for any
one to digest in a day."

- A telegram from Toronto says that a large
conflagration had occurred in that city, and
destroyed an entire block of buildings.
Several English insurance offices are said to be
largely interested in the loss,

We learn froth Australia that the Sussex,
from Plymouth for Melbourne was totally
wrecked just outside Port Phillip Heads on
the 31st of December, when the third officer
and five men were drowned.

Numerous incendiary fires have occurred in
Auckland, New Zealand. Four convicts were
killed in Queensland by lightning in No-
vember.

St. Bartholomew's is to have a Convalescent
Hospital at ifighgate. The house in which
Nell Gwynn lived, situated behind the St.
Pancras Infirmary, and Opposite, to the con-
valescent branoh of the Great Ormond-street
Hospital for Sick Children, has been presented
to the hospital, and will be fitted up to accom-
modate forty or fifty patients.

Mr. Serjettnt Payne died on Sunday in
Brunswick-square. Deceased, who entered
the service of the Corporation of London more
than half a century since, was appointed
coroner of London and Southwark in 1829.
was called to The bar at Orqy's 11111 in 18,0 I
elected High Steward of Southwark and Judge
of the Borough Court of Record in 1850 ; and
created Serjeant at Law in 18;i8.

Sir Charles Dilke was not among the mem-
bers of parliament who were present at the

WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
FOIL PROMOTING THE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO TILE WORKING CLASSES Or GREAT BRITAIN.
FELLOW WORKIIENe--,

The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and state main be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Sessiou
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the House of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. He was met with the objec-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the diseudo wment and disestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for kgislatiee action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Miall, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the Liberation
of Religion front State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as &body, pro.
flounced any judgment on this great question; but.
rit has been felt that, after the broad challenge thrown
Mown by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their honest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
leader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Men, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the Dia-
endowment and Disestablishraent of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a faithful and com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which has been retamed with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These then, are the circumstances under which
_ _

the Working iron's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and
.now proceeds. to work.

The viiws of the Committee may be thus con-
sisely stated—

1.-They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.

2. They are of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been disestablished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
Kingdom
3. They are persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to accomplish the task for which it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Protestantism of the then
State-Church, the groat majority of the. British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish-
ment.

5. The immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation, are distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or leas than half, of the
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries
sod emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Dignitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the tem cat
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations.
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. Jealona
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of a
political or social character, they are always on
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of natiOnal
weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good'men uniting, as
they otherwise might unite, in works of philan-
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affaira of life. '

Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious consideration
of their follow workmen throughout the country.,

In order to ascertain and give effect to their Tie"'
Branch Committees will be formed, and meetings
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and believed,
that the practical result will be that, after this
great question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the HORSE of Commons,
Mr. Miall will be in a position to give to Mr.
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Working
Men's Committee, Yours faithfully,
Gronos Elown.t. (Chairman). ,
DA.NIEL. GUILE (Treasurer).

• Teaching in Elementary Schools, I also consider,

life, and I shall always support any efforts met

ts: nation through the excellence obtained in its

While I hold sincerely to the belief that all

elevated by the inculcation of the great truths o

resist all attempts to give religious teachinge hi

Sectarian propag,andiant. I draw a broad distine•
tion between tliase who seek to teach Cinistirel

for this reason I support in its entirety the Ad-
vanced programme of the Birmingham League
which aims at the establishment of a great smote

On these grounds, Ladies and Gentlemen, I
