SATURDAY, MARCH 2, 1872.

:THE ALL-CLASSES THANKSGIVING.
THE Thanksgiving of 1872, from whatever
point of view regarded, commands our sym-
pathies, and approves itself to our judgment.
Even as a spectacle, the lowest point, it was
truly great, great within the Cathedral, but
far greater without. The multitudinous con-
gregation and the countless concourse were
in the same proportions impressive. Never
did the metropolitan temple of one communion
contain a body of worshippers so universally
catholic before. Never before did any capital
in all the world, no, not London itself, present
such an assemblage, so immense in number,
so patient in spirit, so united in sentiment, so
one in heart.
The scene which presented itself to the eyes
of the QUEEN and her children as they passed
from Palace to Cathedral, and from Cathedral
back to Palace, though cleverly described
in the morning papers, surpassed all powers of
adequate description. Not that the decora-
tions, though good and abundant beyond
example, were overwhelmingly magnificent,
but that the people collected to see, and to be
seen, were, along the whole route, so many,
so gay, so good-humoured, so heartily loyal,
and so comprehensively, as well as so gigan-
I tinily representative of .the whole nation in
all its ranks and classes. Every spot, high or
low, upon which a foot could be set, was occu-
pied by some spectator; every window, every
roof; together with a vast number of stands and
pavilions erected at vacant spaces, far ex-
ceeding in number, size, accommodation,
and adornment, any structures of the kind
heretofore seen. The sum of money expended
on this occasion, in materials and in labour,
would, if it could be counted up and stated,
appear almost incredibly great.
The very weather seemed to betoken a
celestial sympathy in: the occasion. Those
who had struggled through mud and mire the
evening before to take a survey of the street
preparations, pleasantly made their way next
morning to the solemnity upon. pavement dry
and clean, and beneath the rays of a bright
sun. The whole procession went and returned
Under his genishuspices ; and his beams added
to the grouping within the cathedral a crown-
ing brilliancy, the like or lack of which no art
or arrangement could have supplied.
GOD himself best knows how far the hearts
of sovereign, prince, and people, corresponded
to the outward attitude of all who partioipata
in this grand act of thanksgiving. The coldest
and the most sceptical, however, must surely
have been impressed with a something which,
both in the church and under the open sky,
spread itself over the whole assemblage, and
raised the entire Beene to a moral height
infinitely above the sense of being concerned in
more spectacle ever so wonderful and splen-
did.

It was not to be expected that such a scene
Should pass away without any accident to
life ol limb. Every precaution had been
taken at every point which forethought could
suggest, or . active skill and energy provide
against But, in spite of all, the pressure of
crowds or the instability of temporary struc-
tures, occasioned several casualties, a few of
Which required surgical attention; and there
have been reports of at least one death. It
Would be a welcome crown to the satisfactions
of the auspicious day, could both sovereign
and subjects assure themselves that this
memOrable celebration of a restored Prince
passed off without bringing death to the
humblest citizen.
It is a oircutastanoe not unworthy of remark,
that, on the morning of this historic day, our
QUEEN had for guests at her breakfast-table
the man who but lately called himself
EMPEROR of the FRENCH, his wife, and their
son. Howsoever this incident may have
come to pass, it is a striking one—that the
most esteemed of sovereigns should have parted
from a dethroned autocrat, to go and receive
the spontaneous congratulations of a mighty
host, beyond question rep retentative of every
rank, class, and degree of her unconstrained
subjects. It is also a curious counterpart to

this beginning of the day in the Royal Palace,
that the same street which overflows
with a narrative of the whole proCeeding
from midnight to midnight, should apprise
us that, whilst in a Christian Temple,
the most numerhs and the most various
, congregation ever assembled
.since ermsyr ap-
peared, were Pouring out thanks to -Go]) for his
goodness to our QUEEN, our PRINCE, and our
nation, similar acts of gratitude were being
performed, not only •in the 'cities
..of Paris
and Berlin, but even in.those of Calcutta and
Bombay; and not simply in the Christian
churches and chapels of
.our Indian Empire,
but in the Fire 'remples of ,the Parsecs, the
Mosques of the Ma.homedans, and the sacred
edifices of the Hindoos. Facts and circum-
stances like these form an impressive, practical
comment on the comprehensive text of the
Primate's judiciously short discourse, " Mem-
bers one of another ; " as also a lively exempli-
fication' of the PnortEß's remark on the first
day of the Session, that " we live in an age •
when the whole of civilised mankind is
gradually becoming a unit,"
The Minds of. politicians naturally. occupy
themselves in estimating from their point of view
the moral value of this remarkable event. If
everything has its influence, of which there can
be no doubt, then a thing so extraordinary and
unexampled must exert a proportionate power.
It behoves us, however, always' tci bear in
mind, that the most powerful things are liable
to be • checked and counteractel by other
things, sometimes following so soon after as to
arrest the out-going of the consequence first
set in
,circulation long before it has
expended itself around. The display
.of
which many of us arc so proud, and
with so much reason, has, indeed, a twofold
value. It is valuable for what it
,indicate a as
really existing previous to itself.; and it is
further valuable for the future good of which

it may, as it is fitted to be, productive. But
all will do well to °onside* and none morello
than those who are sanguine as to what shall'
follow, that it is only as scorning s are con
verted into realities, and as passing glories
are solidified into permanent benefits, that a
°usual aggregation of individuals can become
a national unity, a single sunbeam expan d
into a universal and everlasting noon.

ATROCITIES OF THE FRENCH
GOVERNMENT.
WE know of few things more shocking than
the accounts we occasionally read in our daily
papers of the trials and punishments of the
Communist prisoners in Franco. If M. Trams
is not accountable for the awful brutalities
perpetrated, he is taking upon himself a load
of infamy from which he will find it difiloult
to get free. And if he can prevent these
horrors, and makes no adequate effort for that
purpose, his guilt is as black as any that ever
fell as a curse on the name of any miscreant
history holds record of.
We know all that can be alleged against
these men, and we are not disposed. to dispute
the charges made against them. Ilut granting
they were as bad as the most unscrupulous
amongst their accusers try to make them out,
the treatment they have to undergo in every
form, whether of detention, deportation, con-
finement in fortresses, or shooting, carries with
it every appearance of vengeance, and scarcely
any whatever of justice.
These butcheries committed under cover of
law, these cold-blooded muriers in the out-
raged name of justice, ought to be protested
' against by every civilized government in
Europe. And. if the victims belonged to the
rich and noble, the general outcry would
compel those who are now pursuing this evil
course to hold their hands. It was bad enough
when at first we read of tens of thousands of
prisoners huddled together in a most brutal
manner, suffering privations and miseries as
bad as those of the Libby prison, without trial or
chance of trial for months; and it could scarcely be
called an improvement when they wore dragged
before the tribunals, set up for their trial, but
which might be more truly said to be instituted
for their condemnation. And even the severe
sentences, when short of death, could scarcely
be considered as an augmentation of their
misfortunes, as most people felt that by
reyolution, or by a re-awalcening of humanity

in the nation, some kind of commutation must
at no very distant period come to relieve their
sufferings. •
But what are we to think of those terrible
scenes at Satory, the sickening details of
which were described in the papers
last week? I;rEnnArinun fell stout, dead,
his face almost blown away. lIERPIN
rolled back two yards, and writhed about
with horrible spasms and contortions.
LAGRANGE, mutilated in his lower limbs,
struck about wildly_ with his, right baud.
At length two senior sergeants went up to them
and fired the contents of their pistols into their
heads, and so ended the Satory performance
in defence of order. We qn9te literally from
the Daily News, and it would be impossible to
add in any way to the horror of such a narra-
tive.

Surely this blood cannot sink into the earth
without bearing the
,bad fruit of revenge.. Its
shedding cannot depend for its punishment on
any political section of the
.French *pig.
Such outrages on humanity must be resented
by mon of all sections of the community. The
merett sense of what is duo by man to.man,
the faintest recognition of human brotherhood
and duty, will arm men against such atrocities.
It may be that in England we have no right
to interfere with the actions 'of the French
Government, but as men we may remonstrate,
as Christian and civilized men, we may. lift up
our voices against them.

Some member of Parliament really ought to
draw the attention of our Government in some
way to the matter, were it only for the purpose
of making M. TIIIERS aware of the horror and
disgust his tribunals and their doings are ex -
citing. To be silent is, in a certain way, to be
participators in the gilt of such transaetions.
We may be powerless to save, but we can pro-
test. We can at least show that we detest
such cruelties; and this, at least, we are bound
to do, wore it only that thereby we shall have
established our right to protest in the future
should these wickednesses be retaliated by the
party now suffering.

Terrible punishments will most assuredly
follow this blood-guiltiness, and in France at
the present moment, when leading men are
only despicable intriguers, plotting for their
parties, instead of working for their country,
the cleverest and most industrious, instead of
setting up thrones and dynasties, may, in real-
ity, only bo erecting scaffolds upon which
they themselves- may have to expiate their
crimes.

articles.title: MR. BRIGHT.
articles.text:
MR. BRIGHT.

IT will be seen from the correspondence pub-
lished in another column, between the com-
mittee, on the part of the leading London
working men, and the Right Hon. JOHN
BRIGHT, M.P., that it is proposed to present
him with a congratulatory address on his re-
storation to health, and his probable return to
publio life. We are glad to learn from the
reply of Me. Brtrairr, that be will consent to
receive the address sometime during the pre-
sent session, and the committee appointed to
carry out the movement have resolved to in-
vite the co-operation of the whole of the work-
ing men of London, without reference to
seotion or parties, so as to be prepared to
present the address when gr. 13nionT is will-
ing to reeeive it, and in a rammer which ho
may approve..

From the tone of the Press throughout the
country, the proposal meets with general ap-
proval and commendation, as will be seen from
the following extract, taken from the Leeds
Mercury, and which is only,one of many

"The determination of• the working :Men of
London to present to Mr. Bright, M.P., an address
of congratulation on his recovery is a thoughtful
and generous act, and we can only regret that the
time has not yet come when the presentation can
be made in the form 'which both the working men
and Mr. Bright wish it to take. The right hon,
gentleman has recovered, but he does not yet feel
himself strong enough to resume the active duties
of publie life, and he asks, therefore, that the pre-
sentation shall be postponed. This postponement
will enable the committee who have charge of the
address to secure further signatures to it, and to
hulk° it a thoroughly representative rather than a
political address. Pew men have deserved' mom
at the hands of the working classes than Mr.
Bright. His life has been devoted to the promo-
tion of ,their political interests and indirectly to

their social improvement, There is scarcely any
groat popular movement of recent times which
be has not championed, and ho has lived
to see
,representation founded upon the
broad and simple basis of taxation. In
,a few months the Ballot 'will bare been added to
the list of reforms which he has spent himself in
achieving. Ire has worked with untiring zeal:
His great abilities have at all times been placed at
,the command of the people, and the reputation he
.fiasi won- is lie pure and unselfish as it is wide and
powerful. His voice has been missed in the coun-
cils ,of the nation, and his absence from Parlia-
mentary life has been is public misfortune. His
recovery and his return to Parliament .have been
hailed as the harbinger of peace, and the source of
renewed party strength. We regret that he has
not yet been aUcto take his, seat, but it is some
satisfaction to know that he hopes to do so during
the present Session. In the meanwhile we trust
that those who have charge of the address to
which we have referred will carry on the work, so
that when the time comes forits presentation the
event shall be worthy of the working classes and
of Mr. Bright."

We understand that the committee will
shortly. invite the trades and other associations
of working men to a meeting to discuss the
details, and make the necessary arrangements
for carrying the movement out in a successful
manner, worthy of the man and creditable
to the.cause.

articles.title: _STATISTICAL RESULTS OF THE
articles.text:
THE
_STATISTICAL RESULTS OF THE

CONTAGIOUS DISEA.SES ACTS.

A very important paper upon this subject was
read before the Medical Society of London, on
Monday evening last, by Dr. Charles Bell Taylor.
The writer showed that the English army; as a
whole, was in a worse state, as regarded the special
diseases against which those Acts were levelled,
in the year 1869, the last year for which the
Official Reports of the Health of the Army have
as yet been published, than in 1866, the year before
the Acts were brought into operation. He showed,
also, that the number of eases of those diseases
occurring in the Navy at Home Ports, in the year
1869, was as great as in the year 1866. lie pro-
nounced the Acts, in consequence, a total failure in
a sanitary point of view. There was a largo at-
tendance of eminent medical men present upon
the occasion, including one member of the late
Royal Commission, and many of the witnesses
examined before it.

FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

A meeting was held on Wednesday evening at
the Vestry Hall, Chelsea, for the purpose of con-
sidering the advisability of instituting a club to be
devoted to the interests of the friendly societies of
the south-west district. The object in view of the
promoters is to provide some fitting accommodation
for the poorer classes who mostly congregate in
public-houses to consider any matters connected
with their welfare. 'oresters, Odd Fellows,
Anent Buffaloes, and others have hitherto held
their councils in the smoky and beery atmosphere
of the shrine of Bacchus. This is not conducive

and other matters for consideration. Hence the

THE GOVERNMENT AND THE BALLOT
BILL.

The deputation from the Tower Hamlets Radi-
cal Association and electors waited upon Mr.
Forster on Monday afternoon for the purpose of
suggesting several amendments in the Ballot Bill.
Mr. Forster, in reply to several suggestions, said
he could not consent to make any alteration in
respect to the appointment of returning officers.
The bill, as it now stood, empowered the returning
officer, or his deputy, to order the removal of any
person from a polling booth who he thought had
no right to be present. As to the extension of the
hours for polling, he thought it very undesirable
that any particular candidate should have the ad-
vantage of using the polling place for his special
interest, and the question as to one being used for
the purpose of his election should be considered.
He would do all in his power to support the
amendment to throw legal expenses on the rates.
On the question of paid canvassing, he thought the
Government had gone as far as the House was
likely to sanction in the Corrupt Practices Bill.
A deputation from the Birmingham Labour
Representation League also waited on the Right
lion. W. E. Forster, on Wednesday afternoon.
The deputation consisted of Mr. Monk, the Hon
Secretary of the Birmingham Labour League;
Mr. Bolland, and Mr. Osborne, members of the
executive council of the League; and Mr. Davis.
Mr. Mottershead, secretary of the London Labou
Representation League, and Mr. Facy, a membe
of the London executive, attended the deputation.
The deputation was introduced by Mr. Matters-
head, in the absence of Mr. Dixon, M.P.
Mr. Monk, who was the first speaker, said the
working men of Birmingham, and the working
men of the country generally, were very anxious
indeed that the Ballot Bill should become law, and
they were also anxious that the measure should
be passed in as perfect a form as possible, 80 as to
prevent any unnecessary
tground of complaint or
future agitation on the question. The present
hours of polling, namely, from eight o'clock a.m.
to four o'clock p.m. was altogether unsuitable to
the household suffrage of the present period. The
objection that late voting would lead to riot and
disorder was, in the opinion of the working
classes, more fanciful than real.

Mr. Boßand said the working classes had come
to the conclusion that the Government inserted
clauses into measures which they were not parti-
cularly anxious to pass. The working men con-
sidered it necessary to their interest that the hours
should be altered; they had given certain support
to the present Government, and they expected
something more practical than the old theories.

Mr. Osborne and Mr. Davis also spoke to this
effect, and pointed out the hardships under which
they considered the working daises suffered.

In reply Mr. Forster reminded them that a
provision for extending the hours of polling was
inserted in the Bill that had already been before
Perliament, but was not carried because it was
evident from the divisions which took place that
the majority of the constituencies were not in
favour of it. Mr. Forster was of opinion that any
attempt to carry a similar clause in the Bill now
before the House would impede its passage, and
as the measure was a Ballot Bill, pure and simple
ho desired that nothing should be done that would
bay° that effect. He had no objection to the
agitation apokeh of, and if it .should result in
convincing Parliament the expediency of conduct-
ing elections in the dark, no doubt it would at
some future time be adopted by the Legislature
With reference to a proposal to charge the legal
expenses of Parliamentary elections on the local
rates, in order, that able men who were poor
might take their share in the government of the
country, the right hon. gentleman said it would
not be necessary to present any further arguments
on the point, because he was strongly of opinion
that the legal expenses should be charged on the
rates. Individually he was of opinion that this
question was really more important than the
question of the ballot; and gentlemen who were
present who imagined that the Government were
not in earnest were altogether mistaken. They
overrated the power of the Government if they
thought they could have compelled the House to
adopt that for which they were contending whiten
accepting one of two alternativcs—viz., riskingt
the passage of the Bill through the Commons, or
adopting the question as one on which the fate of
the Ministry should be allowed to depend. The
people of whom the deputation ought to complain
wore the constituencies. In two instances the
members for Liberal places voted against the
proposal, and he had not heard that their conduct
had been condemned.

articles.title: ECONOMY.
articles.text:
ECONOMY.

The Government has once more started on the
path of economy, and we trust that they will go
forward in the course which they have this year
marked out. The not charge of the Army in the
ensuing financial year is set down at £13,582,000,
being an actual decrease of £1,027,200, as corn.
pared with the outlay on this branch of the
service in 1871. But this sum is still too large
and out of all proportion to the requirements of
the country. A million a week, or something like
52,000,000 a year, ought to be sufficient for the
Army, Navy, Civil Service, and payment of interest
on the National Debt; but we fear it will be some
years before the country will return its steps as
regards the, question of expenditure. With an
array of ironclads, which no other Power can
boast of possessing, for our first lino of defence, we
are still spending on our Army a greater sum than
either Franco or Germany, the two foremost
military Powers of the Continent. The reduction
of more than a million on the year is, however,
it is to be hoped, an earnest of future contractions
in the expenditure of the country.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL STATISTICS OF IRELAND.
articles.text:
AGRICULTURAL STATISTICS OF
IRELAND.

The usual abstractiof the agricultural statistics
of Ireland has been presented to Parliament.
The inquiry conductei by the constabulary last
summer shows 5,620,226 acres under crops,
10,068,818 acres under grass, 22,323 acres fallow,
324,285 acres of woods and plantations, and
4,290,011 acres of bog and waste unoccupied and
with no live stook upon it. This accounts for
20,325,693 acres, and is exclusive of the larger
rivers, lakes, and tideways. The area under grass
and green crops continues to increase, and the
area under cereal crops continuos to decrease.
Oats, however, still occupy 1,633,960 acres.
Meadow and clover account for 1,827,733 acres,
and potatoes, 1,058,287 acres; flax has declined to
156,883 acres. The returns of live stock in 1871
show 537,633 horses, the number having gradu-
ally increased in the last five years, and the in-
crease in 1871 over 1870 being nearly five thou-
sand; cattle, 3,073,102, showing the large increase
of above 173,000 over 1870, and of half a million
in the last ton years ; pigs, 1,616,754, an increase
of more than 155,000 over 1870, and of half a
million in the last ten years. The number of sheep
is 4,228,721, being 108,000 fewer than in 1870,
but still showing an increase of nearly 700,000 in
the ten years, The Registrar-General mentions
that in July last he submitted to the Lord.
Lieutenant a return stating the nunAter of
thoroughbred and other sires in Ireland in 1864,

SUNDAY LABOUR, IN POST-OFFICES.
The Committee, consisting of Lord Dalhousie,
Sir George Grey, and Mr. Monsell, who were ap-
pointed to inquire into Sunday labour at the
Post-office, have presented their report to Parlia-
ment. They are of opinion that there should be
made more favourable conditions for the discon-
tinuance of a Sunday post. They propose that a
Sunday rural post shall be taken off if the re-
ceivers of two-thirds of the letters for the district
desire its discontinuance, and that no Sunday rural
post shall be put on unless the receivers of two-
thirds of the letters for the district desire its esta-
blishment, or (as the case may be) its restoration,
They think that the practice of making a Sunday
delivery to callers at the Post-office, in place of a
house delivery, is objectionable. They suggest
that the work of collection on Sundays might be
restricted.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMEND KENT

AOT.

On Tuesday, the Nottingham Trades Union
Association, numbering about. thirty members, re-
presenting sixteen trades, composed of about 3,000
trade unionists, met the Hon. Auberon Herbert,
M P., at tho Talbot lan, Nottingham, to obtain
his opinions, and ask the hon. gentleman to use his
best endeavours to get the law repealed.
Mr. Charles Warburton, President of the Asso-
ciation, introduced the hon. gentleman.
Mr. Herbert said—r. Chairman and gentle-
men, I 'am very glad to have this opportunity of
meeting you to-night, for I am very much pleased
to meet anyone in a friendly discussion, such as I
hope we shall have this evening ; but I come not
so much to give my. opinions upon the bills in
question, as to hear what you have to say. If you
think there is anything at all important as an
alteration or amendment, I hope you will tell me
without the least reserve. I don't want to make
speeches, but to tell one another what we think,
in as plain and simple a manner as possible. I
think if these meetiogs were carried on.. in that
manner they might be made both interesting and
profitable. I think this way of meeting, and your
telling me anything you feel, would be very valu-
able helps to us both. I will gladly exchange
opinions with you, but I would rather have your
Opinions upon the Bills in question than give you
mine. What I say to-night I say under the greatest
reserve, because I have never gone fully into this
subject since it was before the House; neither do I
pretend to speak legally, for, as you are well aware,
I was not brought up a lawyer. When the Bill

was in the House, I and a few others did all wo
could to have it passed quite a different Bill to
what it now appears. I think an Act something of
this kind is required, but very different to the one
now in operation. When the Act was under con-
sideration, 1, with several others, made a speech
against it, but they never appeared in the papers.
Yo a would, no doubt, be disappointed (and not
surprisingly either until you know the reason)
that I did not more strenuously oppose the mea-
sure, but I will explain it. As there was such a
pressure of business last session, and debates wore
often kept up until a late hour, the different news-
papers agreed to cut down all the speeches made
after a certain time, and so if any member made
a speech after twelve o'clock, the papers said the
next morning that Mr. So-and-so addressed the
House, or that:the member for such a place next
spoke, and expressed snob an opinion. So I spoke
for nearly an hour, and so did Mr. 3lundella, but
all that appeared was that we addressed the House
Upon the Bill. My opinion is still the same as the
one I expressed in my speeches to the Government,
and as I said then I say now, although under the
greatest reserve, that if any man is to be
punished, it must be clearly proved that he has
been guilty of some criminal and punishable
offence. No man ought to be punished except he
himself feels that it is a wrong and wicked action;
Mr. Glyn, the opposition Whip, was greatly
astonished that I did not take the aide of the
Government, but I told him one man was not
Obliged to follow another without ho felt well
satisfied in his own mind that it was quite right,
but did not follow with the man he generally did,
there was no reason that he should leave the people
unacquainted with it, and so I explained to Mr.
Glyn. I think myself, and I believe that it is
Your hearty belief, that the unions generally do
not believe in, neither are they in a position to
commit, ,these acts of violence, and should they be
perpetrated, the people they most hurt are them-
selves. I think we cannot show to the people
outside too plainly that tho unions do not want to
coerce anyone. The Act is simply against the
man who commits any violence or creates any
disorder, and he should be punished. I am sure
You are prepared to follovelthat as far as it
goes. Again, the, man who does any wrong,
Whether he is a unionist or a brawler, ought to
be punished. But, as I said before, I came here
more to hear your ideas upon the question than
to give my own. Will you kindly give me
yours now?

Mr. Aston said the association has been formed

Tho flQn, A..llerbert IQ—Undoubtedly there

would have the power to claim 4amages, and to
prosecute for breach of laws, but you would
also incur greater respousibilities than you
do now. But if you make up your minds
to be placed- on tho same footing as
the joint stock companies are, I think you might.
get that altered. But the difficulty merely sprang

vote passed (but I am a little afraid of giving my

Criminal Amendment Act, it, I think, wants

which might be greatly amended. But, in
fact, I think perhaps it might be repealed
altogether. I don't
,know what the Trades
Unionists in Nottingham mean to do as
regards this Bill, but Nrii Meyer is done I will give

believe Mr. Seely presented a petition against this

for you.

INEPORTANT TRIAL.

On Tuesday a case, involving a point of much
importance to trades unions, camo up at tho Small
Debt Court, at Airdrie, before Sinnifl Login. An
action was brought by Edward Burns, a working
mason, to recover pocuniary damages from four
fellow-workmen, named respectively Crosby,
Lockhart, APLay, and Gattiner, as compensation
for loss sustained by him through his being de-
prived of employment by an unlawful combination
on their part, they having told his employers that
if he was not discharged from the employment
they would quit work, in consequence of which
the pursuer was dismissed. • •

Mr. T. A. Macfarlane appeared as agent for the
defenders, and stated the defence to he a denial
that the men had unlawfully combined for the
purpose alleged. Proof was accordingly led at
some length, Mr. Rose conducting Lease for
pursuer. - -

Pursuer, on being examined, deponed that he
had been in the employment of Messrs. Gibson
and Goldie, builders, Coatbridge, since May last.
The whole of .the defenders wore in the same em-
ployment. On the 22nd January last Crosby told
pursuer that he must pay down 7s. 6d. for the
society. Pursuer did not know what kind of
society it was—it was not a sick society. Ho
, never saw the rules of it, though ho had paid for
them. Ho did not know the name of the society;
but ho had joinod it about the time he went to
that employment. The four defenders and pur-
suer were all the workmen Messrs. Gibson and
Goldie employed. On the 23rd January the de-
fenders came out to work, but did not commence.
They went outside of the gate, and Mr. Gibson
followed and spoke to them. On coming back,
Mr. Gibson told pursuer that "they had all struck
against him;" and though he was sorry to part
with him, stilt he would have to dismiss him.
Pursuer was dismissed on the spot—it being the
rule ia the work that no notice la required to

break the engagement. Pursuer asked Lockhart,
one of the defenders, what was wrong; and he
answered that they were not going to work unless
he (pursuer) loft, or joined the society.
Mr. Macfarlane, for defenders, said in opening

_
he thought it necessary to state that it was
doubtless the opinion of many of them, as it was
of himself, that the_presont law in regard to coin,
binations among. workmen should he very mach
altered. What Mr. Rose had said about the rights
of working men was rather what they would Wish

to see than what actually did exist. In reference
to what had been said in regard to the common
law of the land, he might be allowed to state
what he understexl such to be. At common law,
a party was entitled to do anything which was
consistent with his legal rights, no matter what
might be the c3osequence to another. Mr. Mae--
Evian° quoted authorities in support of this posi-
tion, and argued that the act of the defenders was
quite legal, even supposing that all that was
alleged against them wera true. The Trades'
Union Act, he said, had made it a matter of per-
fect legality for working men to combine for the
purpose of giving, withholding, or regulating
labour, repealing the old. law which rendered
illegal any combination for restricting trade. It

WM Stated that these men in an unlawful com-
bination went to their nrtsters and said that unless
Burns was paid off they would not work. This
was a simple withholding of their labour, which
was quite a legal act; and ho contended that there
was not a distinct threat mtained in what these
men were alleged to have said.

Sheriff Logic, in a very long speech, gave his
decision. He slid the question raised was
exceedingly important, an I more especially so to
the working classes themselves. n was not a
question as to whether it was lawful for working
men to combine to force their masters to pay them
a higher rato of wages; that was a perfectly legal
act. The questions he had to determine were—
Whether it was lawful for workmen to go to their
employers and say, "We are quite willing to
continue work, on, condition that a person whom.
we don't like is expelled ;" and whether the per,
son so expelled is entitled to sue for damages.
From the importance of the question, he thought
he should look very carefully into the authorities
on the subject 'before giving his decision. He
thought it would be a great pity if working men,
or any class of them, should have the power to force
men into a society which they did not wish to join.
He said : I have carefully perused the recent ease
of Weardon, to which .I
was referred by the agent
for the defenders, in which the conviction of a
stone-mason at I3olton for molestation was quashed,
but it appears to me to have no hearing on the
present ease, because in that case the prosecution
was a criminal one against Weardon under the
same act for conduct similar to that followed by
the present defenders, and the Recorder held, and
I think rightly held, that he had not boon guilty
of such violorce or intimidation as rendered him
amenable to the criminal law, and he therefore
quashed the decision of the Magistrates. In the
-circumstances of this case, as proved in evidence,
I ant of opinion that the pursuer is entitled to '
darnves from the defenders for haring illegally
combined to coerce their masters to dismiss him Oi
the manner already detailed;, and that the pursuer
having not only lost his employment, but having
been unable to find it elsewhere, as appeared from
the evidence when the case • was heard on e3th
February current, that he 14.3 entitled to £3 3s. of
damages, for which sum I deseera against :the
defenders jointly and severally., with expenses. ,

articles.title: PROPORTIONAL REPRESENTATION.
articles.text:
PROPORTIONAL REPRESENTATION.

Mr. Thomas Hare has published the follow-
ing observations upon what he calls the "re-
markable progress in representative reform,"
which is now being made in New York State.
He says :

, The Committee of Seventy, which was or-
ganised at the great raass meeting of last Sep-
tember in Now York, to investigate the frauds
that had been committed in the city adminis-
tration and generally to take steps to secure
4 good local government for the future, after
mature deliberation, determined almost unani-
mously to adopt a method of proportional
representation. A. sub-committee of fifteen
was appointed, to which the preparation of a
draught charter was confided. This charter,
after having been approved by the Seventy,
was brought before the Legislature of the
State. The joint committee of the cities,
appointel by the two Houses, met the sub-
committee of the Seventy in the Senate Cham-
ber on the 25th of January. The new charter
was then explained by Governor Salomon. He
stated that all the members of the committee
agreed that party spirit ought not to be
allowed to control the municipal or business
affairs of ..t&ew York. Proportional represen-
tation was felt to be the true principle which
should be introduced. That principle was
adopted in the proposed charter. Forty-five
aldermen are to be elected, nine being
chosen from each one of the senatorial dis-
tricts. Suppose in each district there were
18,000 voters, then every 2,000 are entitled
to an alderman to represent them. The honest
men among the inhabitants, by thus uniting
their strength, would acquire a numerical
force sufficient to give them representation.
The principle had recently been adopted in the
election of the school boards in England, and.
in America its operation was seen in the elec-
tion of members of the Assembly in the State
of Illinois, and in the borough officers of
Pennsylvania; and only
.a few days ago the
same method had been proposed to be adopted
in the amendment of the constitution of Wis-
consin. It would be a check on parties and
factions in the selection of candidates. At
present the party candidate must be supported,
or the voter must either abstain altogether or
attach himself to the opposite party. By
adopting this principle he is not forced to
such an alternative. Better men would be
nominated and chosen. None, by being left
in a hopeless minority, would be rendered in-
active. All would be encouraged to select the
men of their choice. The principle was
oarried throughout the proposed charter. The
business of the city was to be divided into
departments—as the Department of Public
Works, of Public Docks, of Parks, of Public
I Safety, of Charities, of Correction, and the
Finance Department. These departments were
to be composed, some of five and some of six
membEra, the chair's an cf each department to be
appointed by the Mayor, and the other members
elected by the Common Council on the same
system of proportional representation. In the
Department of Public Instruction there were
to be thirty members or commissioners—six
for each senatorial district. The Charter was
supported by Mr. Simon Sterne, another
member of the Committee of Seventy, whose
writings on proportional representation are
known in this country. He cited a passage
from the current number of the American Law,
Review :—,‘ A political contest is a struggle,
not for a fair share of the representation, but
for the whole. The outvoted electors have no
voice in political affairs. It is a war without
quarter; and it is a contest in which the
sacrifices of the victors are hardly less serious
than the losses of the defeated party. Every-
thing has to be yielded for the sake of the
vietory, and as eligibility becomes the prime
quality in a candidate, men of eminence give
place to others, and the assembly comes to be
composed for the Most part of second-rate men,
hardly more acceptable to many who vote for
them than to their opponents." He quoted
also an article in the Times, which, referring
to the principle adopted in the late school
board elections in this country, observed that
"those who fight against that principle fight
against light." The subject as still under
discussion in the Legislature of the State of
New York. It will, no doubt, be interesting
to many to see the progress of this great step
in municipal government.

The day of National Thanksgiving,whieh had
boon anticipated with such absorbing interest
for so many weeks, passed off on Tdesday
amid universal expressions of congratulation;
The weather was: all that could be desired.
The early morning was gloomy, but with the
advan cc of the forenoon the blonds gradually
rolled. away, and at intervals during the
passage of the procession, the sun shone out
upon the gay and busy scene, and lit up with
animation the faces of the hundreds of thou-
sands of spectators who formed in dense
masses along the line of route, and occupied
every available position from which a view of
the pageant could be obtained.
Tuesday *as not only a national holiday,
but a brilliant and successful holiday. The !
demonstration was . the mott imposing and

Magnificent which this generation ha's witnessed.
The groat clingy metropolis never in modern
days wore a more thoroughly holiday look.
The decorations of the street were more than
usually elaborate; the crowds were larger than
those which gathered to welcome the Princess
Alexandra when she came from over the sea
to her now island home; and their behaviour
was characterised by that great good humour
which, to do them justice, English crowds
always show. It can no longer be said, after'
Tuesday, that English people do not know how
to get up a show. All the householders and
all the public bodies along the line of route vied
with one another in doing honour to the occa-
sion. Such a profusion of flags and decorations
was never seen in London before. There was
something exceedingly striking in this holiday
aspect of the metropolis. The traffic of the
great thoroughfares entirely stopped, the
shops, the banks, the warehouses, .all the
places of business shut, and the whole popula-
tion turning out to make an English holiday:
And charapteristioally, English it was, the
national festival of a self-ruled and self-re-
specting people.
The Queen, and all the members of the
Royal Family who took part in this extra-
ordinary Spectacle, arrived in London on
Monday night. At ton o'clock on Tuesday
morning the ox-Emperor and Empress of the
French, accompanied by the Prince Imperial,
breakfasted with her Majesty at Buckingham
Palace, and an hour afterwards the Prime
and Princess of Wales, with their two eldest
sons., drove from , Marlborough-house to the
Palace amid tremendous cheering from the
assembled multitude.

From the break of day the ordinary vehi-
cular traffic had. been diverted from the City,
and from a very early hour vast numbers of
persons crowded towards the thoroughfares
whit% had been marked out to be traversed
by the procession, while heavily-laden excur-
mon trains frdtn the country added their quota
to the constantly-gathering throng. As early
is seven o'clock a large prop or tion of ticket-
holders had taken their seats in the windows
commanding a view of the scene, and as time
passed slowly on, these, with the balconies,
the huge erections which were raised in every
available place overlooking the line of route,
the temporary galleries which were run up so
speedily, and in many eases even the tops of the
houses, 'became filled with people. From first
to last the crowd in the streets was enormous,
and at times the line of police, the line of
sentries, and even the cavalry patrols gave
way before the irresistible pressure of the vast
masses of hunian beings, which for number
have never had a parallel in London.
gvery variety of adornment was brought
into requisition for the deooration:of the houses
along the miles and miles of route. This was
more especially the case in the' City, and the
spectaelelooking eastivard from Temple-bar,
will never be forgotten by these who.witneseed
It. Banners floated from the house-tops,
stretched in seoiles across Fleet-street, and
waved in hundreds from the windows, while
the number and character of the devices for
the illuminations testified alike to the spon-
taneous nature of the demonstration, and to
the cordiality with which the capital was pre-
pared to welcome the. Prince of Wales back to
life after a long and dangerous illness.
Shortly before twelve o'clock the processiou
set out from Buckingham Palace, and from the
start until the return its progress was made
amid the most enthusiastic cheering from the
concourse of on-lookers. - The Speaker of the
House of Commons was closely followed by the
I.Ard. Chancellor And the Duke of Cambridge,
his Royal Highness being attended by.a cavalry
Swart. The first seven carriages, containing
the members of the Royal Household, passed
rapidly along, but the oheeriug was long and
loud when the eighth carriage, with the Duke
of. Edinburgh, Prince Arthur, Prince Leopold,
and Prince George of Wales, came into view.
The applause became deafening. when the
people recognised in the next carriage the'
Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales, the
Princess Beatrice, and Prince Albert Victor,

_
All the way along Pall Mall and the Strand
the vast congregations whioh had assembled
showed their loyalty. At Temple Bar her
Majesty- was met by the Civic deputation,
headed by the Lord Mayor, who went through

the ceremony of offering to the Soverei,gn tho
insignia of authority over the City. These
were, as usual, returned, and then his lord-
ship, with the Sheriffs and a number of
Aldermen and Common Councilmen, preceded
her Majesty's carriage on horseback to St.
Paul's, which had been opened to the possessors
of tickets at eight o'clock in the morning.
The Cathedral was reached at a few minutes
to one. As the Royal Family entered the
building the National Anthem was played,
and then followed the Ti Deunt, one of the
two pieces composed by Mr. Goss specially for
the Thanksgiving Service. The sermon was
preached by the Archbishop of Canterbury,
from the text, "Members one of another"
(Roman xii., 5), and the Thanksgiving Hymn,
which followed, was joined in heartily by the
congregation.
On leaving the Cathedral the procession
returned to Buckingham Palace by way
of Ludgate-hill, the Old Bailey, the Hol-
born Viaduct, Holborn, Oxford-street, the
Marble Arch, Hyde-park, and Constitution-
hill, amid displays of loyalty and enthusiasm
similar to those which had greeted the cortege
on its eastward passage.
When, at night, the illuminations were lit
up, the people literally filled the long lines of
streets. From dusk until a late hour the
main Cy thoroughfares were thronged with
"countless swarms of people flocking west-
ward. The City proper had apparently small
attractions for sightseers, as the illuminations,
though in some cases extremely effective,
were few and. far between. It was generally
expected that there would be a grand display
at the General Post-office in St. Martin's Le
Grand? as the extensive apparatus used on
such occasions was ready to hand in the build-
ing, but it so happened that not a single gas
jet beyond and above those used every night
was lighted up. Aldersgate-street was dark
and drear but for an occasional star, and at
long intervals a Prince of Wales Feather and
so on. The most noticeable feature there was
the never-ending stream of humanity pouring
in from the north and, turning westward to
the respective lines of route of the morning's
procession. In Cheapside a marked improve-
ment was visible. Half way down the length
of the street, magnesium lights, gas jets' and
crystal glass stars transformed night into day.
The London Stereoscopic Company and
several of the neighbouring firms, inckding
that of Mr. Sheriff Bennett, made a very
striking and effective display with gas and
coloured fires. The Corporation, who under-
took the illumination of Temple-bar, also
carried out the devices: which ornamented the
Guildhall and the Mansion-house. The former
was resplendent with brilliant jots of gas
running up the flutings of the four pilasters,
while on either side of a largo centre crown
were Prince of Wales' Feathers. The summit
was crowned with three stars. Nothing
remarkable was to be met with until the
Mansion-house was reached. Upon the top of
the cornice and, of the pediment were loyal
mottoes in gas, On each side of the portico
were two stars, and between the columns were
gas standards. In the centre was a large crown
on either side of which were feathers and. stars.
The brilliancy of the Mansion-house was
rivalled by that 'of the Bank of England, both
edifices being thrown into strong relief by the
grim blackness of the Royal Exchange, along
whose front no light was visible. Among the
lanes and alleys of the City there was nothing
to be seen but an isolated star, and the only
grand display further east was made at the
Fishmongers' Hall, from which ancient build-
ing a flood of light was shed upon the shoals
of South Londoners that unceasingly traversed
London-bridge and mingled with the tide
turning westward.

articles.title: SERIOUS ACCIDENTS.
articles.text:
SERIOUS ACCIDENTS.

A number of accidents unfortunately oc-
curred on Tuesday. At about half-past nine
at night the crush westward of Temple-bar
was very great, and caused many persons to
turn into Essex-street to avoid it. Such,
however, was the violence of the mob, that an
elderly man was thrown down, and nearly
twenty persons fell upon him. At length the
sufferers wore extricated, the poor man re-
ferred to being taken up as dead. He was
removed to the Essex Head public-house, and,
after receiving medical au', was taken to
King's College Hospital. The other victims
were removed, some to the George
Hotel, in Devereux-court, in a fainting
condition and bruised, and others to the shop
of Mr. Tozer, Chemist, of Essex-street, and
as late as eleven o'clock some of the un-
fortunate persons 'were unable to proceed to
their homes. Applications for missing friends
and relatives were nontinually being made at
the hospitals. The accident list at King's
College Hospital at half- past ten num-
bered over twenty—broken legs, arms, and
other injuries being among the list. At seven
o'clock there had been seven eases admitted at
St. Bartholomew's Hospital, but none of thorn
of a serious nature. A large stand, capable of
accommodating 150 persons, was erected near
Marlborough House, and at about half-past
twelve o'clock in the afternoon it was occupied
by about ntliety persons. The procession
having prisssd, the masses of people surround-
-ing the structure then surfieds and the QOOll-

pants of the stand became alarmed, and
rushed from one side to the other. In the
excitement and confusion that prevailed, the
crowd rushed against the boirds forming the
stand, and in consequence of the excessive
pressure the whole of the structure was
brought to the
.ground. Several persons re-
ceived severe injuries; one of them was
removed to Westminster Hospital. Many
others occurred.

articles.title: COLONIAL EMIGRATION.
articles.text:
COLONIAL EMIGRATION.

On Tuesday night, Mr. Madre, the Member
for Leith, raised the question of assisted emi-
gration, in a speech as remarkable for lucidity
as it was judicial and able; and although the
Government did not grant the Committee moved
for, they are evidently not insensible to the
merits of the subject. The question was well
ventilated, however, and the debate referred to
has again brought up pretty well all that can
be said on both sides. Mr. Mactio deplored
the outflow of labour to the United States in-
stead of to our own Colonies, and he might
have added, the new-born preference in the
colonies, especially in New Zealand, for Ger-
mau emigrants over those from the mother
country, whilst pauperism, till lately, has
been greatly on the increase. He also gave
due prominence to the fact, that while the
colonies had enriched hundreds of thousands
of our countrymen that commenced on no-
thing, our colonists were our best oustomors.
It was likewise of importance, if we would
preserve our place among nations, that we
should fully occupy the ground we now pos-
sessed, at all events, to the extent of prevent-
ing pauperism and crime, so far as these may
be thus forestalled; and, certainly, if there is
a greater folly under the sun than another, it
is that of creating burdens for our own backs,
as We have been doing. As to the counter
arguments, they were literally threadbare, and
people should be ashamed to use them. We
are aware that so far as Victoria, Tasmania,
New South Wales, South Australia, Queen's
.land, and New Zealand are concerned, they
are able to pay for, and consequently
entitled to select what labour they require.
But this does not apply to Souhtern Australia,
whose area is equal to that of Spain and France
combined, and `whose population is only 26,000.
Its climate is the best in the Southern hemis-
phere, and on this account, as well as its greater
proximity to India, it has often been pointed
out as in every way adapted for a sanitorium to
Europeans in the East. It has every variety
of vegetation and great miwral wealth, not to
mention its suitableness for the breeding of
horses as well as cattle and sheep; yet, strange
to say, while we have labour at home starving
for want of employment, here is a country
starving for want of labour. It seems as if we
preferred hurting ourselves to benefitting the
colony—we ought rather to say, to doing it
bare justice. For, first of all, we made it a
penal settlement, its principal dependence,
then, being on the expenditure of Government;
but thanks to the sister Colonies, it has been
deprived of this resource, and the old respect-
able settlers are suffering immensely from a
curtailed currency and insufficient moans of
communication.

articles.title: PRISON LABOUR.
articles.text:
PRISON LABOUR.

On Monday night, a public meeting was
held at the Lambeth Baths, for the purpose of
considering the "unfair competition" of
prison labour with free labour. Colonel
l3eresford, M.P., occupied the chair, and in
opening the proceedings, said the meeting was
convened for protesting against the utilisation
of prison labour for the purpose of trade. In
his judgment the introduction of trades in
prison labour was a step in the right direction,
and it was much better than keeping prisoners
at hard labour. It was, however, a fact that
hard labour was a greater deterrent to convicts
than any other labour, and if they were to
dispense with it altogether there would be an
increase in crime. They had that evening to
consider three points, which he believed they
would complain of. They complained first of
all of the application of steam power in ono
prison—Wakefield. They complained in the
second place of goods being sold under the
market price; and in the third place they
complained that a larger portion of prisoners,
especially at Wakefield, were employed in the
matting trade than were engaged in any other
trade.

Mr. Adams made a statement, showing how
the matting trade was injured by the labour of
prisoners in relation to public trade.
Mr. Morley, M.P., then addressed the
meeting. He believed that their case was a
hard one, and one which needed a remedy. If
they could make their prisons self-supportingi
he thought it would be an advantage in the
present state of taxation. He took it that
although labour was necessary in prison, it
ought not to interfere with any trade. The
great ground of complaint appeared to him to
he in this small fact, that a mat which the
prison authorities could sell at is. the hones
workman could not sell at such a low figure.
On account of that competition many good
people were pauperised, and he would be glad
to assist those who were before himin any waY
in his power.
Mr. ICldger moved the following resolution :
—" That a prompt and earnest appeal be made
to the Legislature for the appointment of a
Committee of Inquiry into the allegations
now made, to the end that honest industry
may have fair play, and that a valuable al-
though small trade may not be ruined." Mr.
Tallack seconded the resolution, which was
unanimously carried.

articles.title: EDUCATION ACT.
articles.text:
THE EDUCATION ACT.

The following is the resolution which Dlr.
Dixon intends to move in the House of Com-
mons, on the sth of March, at the request of
the National Education League :
That, in the opinion of this House, the provi-
sions of the Elementary Education Act are defec-
tive, and ifs working unsatisfactory, inasmuch
as—

1, It fails to secure the general election of School
Boards in towns and rural districts.

2. It does not render obligatory the attendance
of children at school.

3. It deals in a partial and irregular manner
with the remission and payment of school fees by
School Boards.

4. It allows School Boards to pay fees out of
rates levied upon the community to denomina-
tional schools, over which the ratepayers have no
control.

5. It permits School Boards to use the money of
the ratepayers for the purpose of imparting dog-
matic religious instruction in schools established
by local boards.

6. By the concession of these permissive powers,
it provokes religious discord throughout the coun-
try, and by the exercise of them it violates the
rights of conscience.

Mr. Forster has given notice that upon Mr.
Dixon's motion he will move the following
amendment : _ -

That, in the opinion of this House, the time
that has elapsed since the passing of the Act of
1870 and the progress that has been made in the
arrangements under it are not such as to enable
the House to enter with advantage on a review of
its operation.

To the Editor of the BEE-1-Ltve.

,piece; they do not
